The most visible neoclouds can require some upfront payment, and chips might not come online for months, because providers raise funding based on contracts and set up the data center equipment, Bernhardsson said.

## Baby neoclouds

If companies want GPUs immediately, they might have to go beyond the name brands. Some neoclouds aren't household names because they target specific countries, which can be viable in certain cases. 

"Capacity right now is tight, and your relationships with your suppliers is actually one of the most closely guarded secrets for companies like ours," said Zhen Lu, CEO of Runpod.

Specialist neoclouds can offer more flexibility than the larger GPU clouds, which often require upfront payments and long-term commitments. Some sell so-called bare-metal GPUs, which give customers more control but also require them to manage more of the technical work themselves. 

Companies using these smaller neoclouds share the same concerns: When can they get the GPUs, and at what price? Sunny Smith, co-founder and technology chief at Massed Compute, said customers are often willing to commit to capacity when they expect prices to rise.

...

Amanda Andrade-Rhoades | The Washington Post | Getty Images

The hourly spot price for an Nvidia B200 GPU has more than doubled since March, according to data from Ornn, a startup that maintains indexes.

Collaboration software maker Dropbox Add To Watchlist relies on GPUs in its data centers, CEO Ashraf Alkarmi said. 

"If we want to do a lot more, I think our supply chain connections will still be beneficial and a structural advantage," he said. 

Everpure Add To Watchlist, which sells data center storage hardware and software, has acquired its own GPUs, to run open-weight AI models for the company's software engineers, said CEO Charlie Giancarlo.

"In a very dynamic pricing environment, it's always good to have multiple sources that you can go to," he said.

results.title: AI is easy. Production is hard. | Massed Compute
results.author: Massed Compute
highlights:
A few weeks back our SVP of Global Sales and Revenue Craig Gieringer  joined Hannah Duce of Lightedge and Michael Piccininni of Dell Technologies to talk through what it takes to run AI securely and efficiently at enterprise scale. We pulled the three biggest takeaways into a short read.

1. Start with the use case and get the business owners in the room. One client set on H100s benchmarked first and saved millions with NVIDIA RTX.
2. Benchmark again as workloads move from training to retraining to inference, so spend tracks the real need.
3. Plan for the blind spots. GPU and storage prices doubled over the past year, data prep takes more work than teams expect, and several small pilots build momentum faster than one big bet.

results.title: The compute market is splitting in two.
highlights:
The compute market is splitting in two.

This week, SpaceX was reported to be seeking $40B to buy NVIDIA chips. Days later, news broke that Anthropic and NTT Data are in final talks on a 500MW data center in Osaka that won't partially open until 2028.

When the largest buyers lock up supply and power years in advance, everyone else feels it. Lead times stretch, minimum commitments grow, and the best hardware gets spoken for before smaller teams can even ask.

But the next wave of AI isn't only coming from frontier labs. World models, robotics foundation models, and video generation are being built by startups at much earlier stages. Their compute needs are real and their planning horizon is quarters, not years.
That's who we build for at Massed Compute: dedicated, bare-metal NVIDIA capacity on contracts shaped around a startup's runway.

Curious how others are planning capacity for 2027. Are you reserving early, or staying flexible?

results.title: Nous Research's $90M Round Shows NVIDIA as the Landlord of AI Compute, Not a Stock Picker | AInvest
results.author: Adrian Hoffner
highlights:
Nvidia has been repositioning itself to collect on that traffic rather than merely selling hardware once. Since early July it has offered AI startups a revenue-sharing and credit-support model: instead of financing their own GPU buildouts, companies draw down token credits and cloud operators run large "AI factories" on Nvidia's DSX platform, returning a slice of revenue to Nvidia. Nvidia's chief financial officer, Colette Kress, has called the resulting income a " recurring, usage-linked earnings stream." In August Nvidia went further, partnering with Apollo APO--, BlackRock BLK--, Blackstone BX--, Brookfield BN--, Goldman Sachs GS-- and KKR KKR-- to mobilize more than $500 billion of third-party capital for just such infrastructure 861366--. At the same time, Nvidia and Nous have worked together to make Hermes run natively on Nvidia's RTX Spark chip.

...

The open question is whether that road carries real traffic. The investor Michael Burry has argued that Nvidia's AI investments are circular - capital circulating among the same firms, mining its own demand. The concern attaches to the financing platforms too: Nvidia discloses it may backstop residual value on some opportunities, up to 25% of a project, which could mask a sale to a customer it effectively funded. The signal that would settle it is outside Nvidia's walls. Nvidia's own materials show one-year H100 rental rates rising from about $1.70 per GPU-hour in October 2025 to $2.35 by March 2026, with Blackwell B200 commanding $5.30 to $7.05 - evidence of buyers willing to pay more for increasingly scarce high-end compute. Rising third-party rental prices argue the demand is real; falling rental rates alongside Nvidia backstopping utilization would argue the circularity worry is winning.

results.title: Every Term You Need to Understand AI Compute Pricing
results.author: DataStorage Editorial Team
highlights:
On October 10, 2026, eight NVIDIA H100 GPUs rented as a single node listed at $31.92 an hour on Lambda and $98.32 an hour on Microsoft Azure. Same silicon, same generation, a 3.1x gap. Run either for a month and the difference is $48,472 for one node.

The gap is not a typo and it is not pure margin. It is vocabulary. One quote is an on-demand virtual machine billed per GPU. The other bundles InfiniBand networking, hyperscaler platform integration and an eight-GPU minimum into a node rate. Buyers who cannot tell those apart compare the wrong numbers, sign the wrong contract, and then wonder why the AI budget moved.

...

+16.9% Nebius on-demand H100 increase, effective Oct 1 Nebius, 2026

+38% One-year H100 contract price, Oct 2025 to Mar 2026 SemiAnalysis, 2026

## Why GPU Pricing Vocabulary Matters More in Late 2026

For most of 2025 the story was simple: prices fell. AWS cut on-demand pricing on its H100-based P5 instances by 44 percent in June 2025 (AWS News Blog, 2025). That era is over. SemiAnalysis tracked one-year H100 contract pricing rising from $1.70 to $2.35 per GPU-hour between October 2025 and March 2026, an increase of about 38 percent, as on-demand capacity sold out (SemiAnalysis, 2026). On October 1, 2026, Nebius raised on-demand H100 pricing from $3.85 to $4.50 per GPU-hour and B200 from $7.15 to $8.50, its second increase in a few months (Nebius pricing page, 2026; Stocktwits, 2026).

When prices move in both directions at once, falling on spot marketplaces and rising on contracts, the term attached to the number matters as much as the number itself. Note the source bias too: several widely cited price ranges come from GPU vendors with an interest in making their own rate look cheap. We use first-party price lists wherever possible and say so when we do not.

### GPU-hour

One GPU rented for one hour. It is the common denominator of the market, and almost every comparison table normalizes to it. The trap: a GPU-hour from one provider is not a GPU-hour from another. CPU cores, system RAM, local NVMe storage and network fabric ride along in different quantities. Lambda's 8x H100 instance, for example, ships 208 vCPUs, 1,800 GiB of RAM and 22 TiB of local SSD (Lambda pricing page, 2026). Always ask what comes attached.

...

Hyperscalers and many neoclouds sell H100, H200 and B200 capacity as whole eight-GPU nodes. The per-GPU figure you see in comparison tables is derived by dividing the node rate by eight. If your workload needs two GPUs, a node-only provider still bills you for eight. ... The minimum shape, not the per-GPU rate, sets your minimum bill.

...

### On-demand

Pay as you go with no commitment. The highest list rate, and in 2026 frequently unavailable for top-tier GPUs at the moment you need it. On-demand is a flexibility premium, not a baseline.

### Spot, preemptible and interruptible

Spare capacity sold at a discount that the provider can reclaim. AWS gives a two-minute interruption notice and Google Cloud Spot VMs a default 30 seconds (Spheron, 2026). CoreWeave lists its HGX H100 node at $19.71 per hour on spot against $49.24 on-demand, about 60 percent off (CoreWeave pricing page, 2026). Spot is excellent for checkpointed training and batch inference and a liability for anything stateful or latency-sensitive. The real cost of spot includes the engineering time to make jobs restartable.

### Reserved capacity, Savings Plans and committed-use discounts

A discount in exchange for a one- to three-year commitment. AWS calls them Savings Plans, Google Cloud calls them committed-use discounts, neoclouds usually just say reserved. CoreWeave advertises up to 60 percent off on-demand for committed usage (CoreWeave pricing page, 2026). The catch in 2026: NVIDIA now ships a new data-center generation faster than a three-year term runs, so a three-year commitment on today's chip may lock you into yesterday's price-performance. Short terms and multi-provider strategies have real option value. Our breakdown of reserved, on-demand and spot instances covers the general trade-offs.

### Capacity Blocks

AWS's prepaid reservation of GPU capacity for a fixed future window, from days to weeks. It sits between on-demand and long-term reservations: you guarantee access without a multi-year term. AWS lists p5.48xlarge Capacity Blocks at $47.757 per hour, or $5.97 per H100, against $55.04 on-demand (IntuitionLabs, October 2026). The same report notes the Capacity Block rate rose from $5.19 per H100 between August and October 2026. Prepaid means you pay whether the job runs or not.

...

### Hyperscaler, neocloud, marketplace, broker

Hyperscalers (AWS, Azure, Google Cloud, Oracle) sell GPUs as one service among hundreds. Neoclouds such as CoreWeave, Nebius and Lambda specialize in GPU compute. Marketplaces aggregate capacity from many independent hosts. Brokers resell capacity they do not own. On our podcast, Massed Compute founder Sunny Smith put the first vetting question bluntly: do you own the GPU? Ownership determines who answers the support ticket when a node fails at 2 a.m., and whether that ticket gets copy-pasted between three companies before anyone touches the hardware.

### GPU rental price index

A published daily or weekly benchmark of rental rates for a specific chip. Indices from SemiAnalysis, Silicon Data and Ornn now anchor negotiations the way a fuel index anchors freight contracts. They also expose volatility: B200 rental prices on the Ornn index rose from $2.31 to $4.95 per hour in six weeks in spring 2026 (Tom Tunguz, citing Ornn, 2026). An index is a reference, not your price; it averages away your region, shape and terms.

...

Exchange-traded contracts that let buyers and providers hedge GPU rental prices. CME Group scheduled its first two, Silicon Data H100 Rental Index Futures and Silicon Data B200 Rental Index Futures, for an October 5, 2026 trade date, pending CFTC review. Each contract covers 730 GPU-hours, one month of continuous rental, quoted in dollars per GPU-hour with a $0.01 tick worth $7.30, and settles financially rather than in hardware (CME Group, 2026). For most teams this is a signal rather than a tool: GPU compute is now priced and hedged like a commodity, which means budgets should be planned with commodity-style volatility.

...

Utilization is the share of paid GPU-hours actually doing work. MFU (Model FLOPs Utilization) goes further: the share of the GPU's theoretical compute your model actually uses. Both are where cheap quotes quietly become expensive bills. An eight-GPU node at $3.99 per GPU-hour that sits idle 40 percent of the time costs $6.65 per useful GPU-hour, more than CoreWeave's full on-demand rate. Fix the idle time before you renegotiate the rate.

...

### TCO (Total Cost of Ownership)

The full cost of running compute over its life: hardware or rental, power, cooling, staff, networking, storage and financing. TCO is what you compare when weighing rental against owning or colocating. With a single B300 server costing around $750,000, per Massed Compute, ownership is financial engineering, which is why most of the market rents.

## Worked Example: Decoding Six Real H100 Quotes

Here is what the glossary looks like applied. Six published on-demand or prepaid rates for one eight-GPU H100 node, run continuously for 730 hours, the same unit CME uses for one futures contract. Rates are first-party list prices checked October 10 to 14, 2026.

| Provider and SKU | $ per GPU-hr | Node $ per hr | 730-hr month |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Lambda, 8x H100 SXM instance | $3.99 | $31.92 | $23,301.60 |
| Nebius, HGX H100 (from Oct 1) | $4.50 | $36.00 | $26,280.00 |
| AWS p5.48xlarge, Capacity Block | $5.97 | $47.76 | $34,862.61 |
| CoreWeave, HGX H100 node | $6.16 | $49.24 | $35,945.20 |
| AWS p5.48xlarge, on-demand | $6.88 | $55.04 | $40,179.20 |
| Azure ND96isr H100 v5 | $12.29 | $98.32 | $71,773.60 |

8 x H100 per node, 730 hours continuous, 5,840 GPU-hours. First-party list prices, US regions, checked October 10 to 14, 2026. Excludes storage, data transfer and support.

...

$35,945

AWS on-demand

$40,179

...

Reading the table with the vocabulary above: the Lambda and Nebius rates are per-GPU on-demand list prices from neoclouds. The first AWS row is a prepaid Capacity Block, not on-demand, so it is cheaper than AWS's own on-demand rate but cannot be cancelled. Azure's ND96isr bundles InfiniBand networking into a node-only shape. None of these include storage, data transfer or the cost of idle time.

The practical lesson: the 3.1x spread between the top and bottom rows is real, but utilization moves the bill just as far: a node busy only 30 percent of the time costs 3.3x its list rate per useful GPU-hour. Choosing the cheapest provider saves money once. Keeping the GPUs busy saves it every hour. Current rates for H100, H200, B200 and more are tracked daily in the DataStorage.com GPU Price Explorer.

...

Key Takeaways

- The same H100 node ranged from $31.92 to $98.32 per hour on first-party price lists in October 2026, a 3.1x spread driven by packaging and terms, not silicon.
- GPU prices are moving in both directions: spot marketplaces stay cheap while contract and neocloud on-demand rates rose through 2026, including Nebius's October 1 increase of up to 21 percent.
- Compare effective cost per useful GPU-hour, not list rate. Idle time can erase any provider discount.
- Compute futures on CME turn GPU rental into a hedgeable commodity. Plan AI budgets for commodity-style volatility.
- Keep training data on zero-egress storage so you can follow the cheapest available GPUs without paying to leave.

...
